# Meet Cloudbot

Cloudbot (now called Multi-bot) is an AI assistant that runs on its own computer, usually a Mac mini. Unlike a regular chatbot, it doesn't wait for you to ask it things. It can browse the web, send emails, manage files, and even message you first when something important comes up.

You talk to it through Telegram, so you can manage everything from your phone.

# Keep It Simple: Start With a Mac Mini

You don't need expensive hardware to get started. A cheap used Mac mini or a $25/month virtual Mac rental works just fine.

The nice thing about a Mac is that when Cloudbot gets stuck, you can screen-share in and see exactly what it's doing. Much easier than debugging server logs.

# Setting It Up Is Mostly Copy-Paste

![Cloudbot chat interface](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/claudebot-chat-interface.jpg)

The setup is straightforward: install Homebrew, Node.js, and Multi-bot. Then create a Telegram bot and link your Claude subscription.

Once it's running, send "hi" through Telegram. Cloudbot will introduce itself and you're good to go.

# Daily Check-Ins That Come to You

This is the simplest use case, but maybe the most life-changing. Set up a cron job so Cloudbot messages you every morning asking for your top three priorities. Then at night, it asks what you got done.

It keeps a running log and updates your task list automatically. You never have to open an app or remember to check in.

# It Can Use a Browser on Its Own

Cloudbot can control Chrome autonomously. Ask it to check your latest YouTube video stats, and it opens the browser, navigates to YouTube, finds the data, and sends you the results via Telegram.

It can also do competitor research, monitor websites, and gather data from anywhere you'd normally browse yourself.

# Automatic Task Tracking

![ClickUp task board](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/clickup-task-board.jpg)

Connect Cloudbot to ClickUp and it logs every task you assign, tracks progress, and updates the board automatically.

Your morning priorities become ClickUp tasks, and they move through To Do, In Progress, and Completed without you manually updating anything.

# Teaching It New Skills

![Cloudbot skills dashboard](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/claudebot-skills-dashboard.jpg)

Cloudbot learns new abilities when you give it API keys and point it to the documentation. It reads the docs, builds the integration, and saves it to its persistent memory.

You can be vague with your instructions. It's smart enough to figure out the details on its own.

# How Cloudbot's Memory Works

![Cloudbot architecture](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/claudebot-anatomy-wide.jpg)

Cloudbot has a persistent memory file called soul.md where it stores everything it learns. It also connects to external services through API keys and MCP servers.

This means skills and knowledge survive restarts. Once it learns something, it remembers it for good.

# Email Negotiation on Autopilot

![Sponsorship workflow](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/sponsorship-workflow-diagram.jpg)

Using a service called AgentMail, Cloudbot gets its own email address. Forward a sponsorship inquiry to it, and Cloudbot drafts responses based on your rates and preferences.

The important part: it always asks for your approval before sending anything. You stay in control while it handles the back-and-forth.

# Your Personal Marketing Team

![YouTube analytics](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/youtube-analytics-results.jpg)

When a new YouTube video goes up, Cloudbot can automatically clip it into Shorts using Opus Clip, then publish them across YouTube, Instagram, and X through Blotato.

The entire pipeline runs without you lifting a finger. And because it lives on a Mac mini, it keeps working even when your laptop is closed.

# QA Testing and Code Fixes

Cloudbot can test your website by opening a browser, clicking through links, and reporting anything that's broken. Schedule this as a recurring job for continuous quality checks.

Even better: if Cloudbot has GitHub access, it can fix the issues it finds and push the changes. Detection to fix, without you touching code.

# Control It From Anywhere

![Telegram on Apple Watch](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/telegram-watch-app.jpg)

With TG Watch (a Telegram app for Apple Watch), you can send voice messages to Cloudbot right from your wrist. Jump Desktop lets you see and control the Mac mini's screen from your phone or iPad.

No subscriptions needed for Jump Desktop, just a one-time $15 purchase.

# Keeping It Running 24/7

To make sure your Mac mini never sleeps, go to System Settings and turn on "Prevent automatic sleeping" and "Start up after power failure."

You can also ask Cloudbot to run the caffeinate command as an extra safeguard. That's it. Your always-on AI coworker is ready.

# The Big Ideas

Cloudbot isn't just a chatbot on your phone. It's an autonomous agent with its own identity, running on a persistent computer.

Start with daily check-ins. Teach it skills one at a time. Always require approval for external actions like emails. And layer use cases over time: browser automation plus GitHub access plus cron jobs can become full automated pipelines.

## Overview

Most people think of AI assistants as tools you chat with when you need something. Cloudbot (now called Multi-bot) flips that model entirely. Instead of a passive chatbot waiting for prompts, it's an autonomous AI agent that runs on a dedicated computer — typically a Mac mini — and can do anything a person sitting at that machine could do.

The key shift is from reactive to proactive. Cloudbot has its own identity, controls a browser, manages files, sends emails, and even messages you first when it has something to report. You interact with it through Telegram, meaning you can manage it from your phone, tablet, or Apple Watch from anywhere in the world.

This guide covers eight specific use cases demonstrated by creator Samin Yasar, who uses Cloudbot daily for everything from morning accountability check-ins to automated YouTube Shorts publishing.

## Hardware Setup: Mac Mini vs VPS

There's an active debate about where to run Cloudbot. Some people use a $5/month VPS, others buy a Mac Studio. The practical recommendation: **start with the cheapest Mac mini you can find**, or rent a virtual Mac for around $25/month.

Why a Mac over a VPS? Because Cloudbot sometimes gets stuck, and when it does, you need to visually see what it's doing. With a Mac mini, you can screen-share from anywhere and intervene directly. With a VPS, you're debugging Docker logs at 2 AM. The ability to monitor the screen and take over when needed makes a real difference in practice.

## Step-by-Step Setup

The installation process requires just a terminal and the ability to copy and paste:

1. **Install Homebrew** — The macOS package manager
2. **Install Node.js and npm** — Required runtime dependencies
3. **Install Multi-bot** — The Cloudbot framework itself
4. **Create a Telegram bot** — Via BotFather in Telegram, which gives you a bot token
5. **Configure authentication** — Link to your Anthropic/Claude Code CLI subscription
6. **Enable hooks** — Turn on all three hook options during setup
7. **Skip pre-installed skills** — Easier to configure skills after the daemon is running

Once set up, you can verify by sending "hi" through Telegram. Cloudbot responds with something like: *"I just came online, fresh workspace, no memories yet — who am I, who are you?"*

After setup, the Cloudbot daemon provides a web UI for managing settings, skills, and cron jobs.

## Use Case 1: Proactive Daily Accountability

![Cloudbot chat interface](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/claudebot-chat-interface.jpg)

This is the simplest use case but arguably the most impactful. Instead of you remembering to check in with your task list, Cloudbot messages you first.

The setup: tell Cloudbot to send you a message every morning at 8:30 AM asking for your top three priorities for the day. Then at 10 PM, it asks what you got done and why you didn't finish anything that's left. It keeps a running log and updates a ClickUp task list automatically.

This works through **cron jobs**, which you enable in the daemon's UI. The only additional setup needed is an OpenAI API key for voice transcription (via Whisper), so you can respond to Cloudbot with voice notes instead of typing.

The result: a proactive accountability partner that initiates conversations, tracks your commitments, and maintains a historical log — all without you opening an app or updating a spreadsheet.

## Use Case 2: Browser Automation and Research

Cloudbot can control a Chrome browser autonomously. You send a Telegram message like *"Go to YouTube and look up my latest video's view count"* and Cloudbot opens Chrome, navigates to YouTube, finds the data, and reports back.

This requires loading the Cloudbot Chrome extension:
1. Ask Cloudbot to show you the extension folder in Finder
2. Open Chrome → Extensions → Enable Developer Mode
3. Load the unpacked extension

The browser automation goes beyond simple lookups. You can ask Cloudbot to research competitors, check ad performance across platforms, monitor website changes, or gather data from any site you can access in a browser. When it encounters issues with one approach, it autonomously tries different strategies without being told.

## Use Case 3: Project Management with ClickUp

![ClickUp task board managed by Cloudbot](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/clickup-task-board.jpg)

Once Cloudbot is connected to ClickUp, every task you assign gets automatically logged, tracked, and updated. You can see tasks in To Do, In Progress, and Completed columns — all maintained by Cloudbot without manual updates.

This integrates with the accountability cron jobs from Use Case 1. Your morning priorities get logged as ClickUp tasks, and as you complete them throughout the day, the board updates in real time.

## Use Case 4: Teaching Cloudbot New Skills

![Cloudbot skills dashboard](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/claudebot-skills-dashboard.jpg)

This is where the architecture becomes powerful. Cloudbot doesn't come pre-configured with every integration — instead, you teach it new skills by giving it API keys and telling it to figure out the rest.

The process for adding a new skill (like ClickUp integration):

1. Tell Cloudbot: *"Here's a ClickUp API key. Go to the docs, figure out what it can do, and create a skill so you always log tasks there."*
2. Cloudbot uses its browser to read the API documentation
3. It builds the integration and tests it
4. You tell it to save the skill to its `soul.md` (persistent memory file)
5. The skill is now permanent — Cloudbot remembers it across restarts

![Cloudbot architecture diagram](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/claudebot-anatomy-wide.jpg)

The architecture consists of: **Memory & Context** (soul.md for persistent knowledge), **MCP servers** (for tool integrations), **Authentication** (API keys and service connections), and the **chat interface** (Telegram). You can be intentionally vague when teaching skills — Cloudbot is capable of interpreting imprecise instructions and figuring out the implementation details.

## Use Case 5: Automated Email Negotiation

![Sponsorship workflow diagram](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/sponsorship-workflow-diagram.jpg)

Using a service called **AgentMail**, Cloudbot gets its own email address and can handle sponsorship negotiations autonomously. The workflow:

1. A sponsorship inquiry arrives in your regular inbox
2. You forward it to Cloudbot's AgentMail address
3. Cloudbot drafts a response based on your pre-configured rates and preferences
4. It sends you the draft via Telegram for approval before sending
5. The back-and-forth negotiation continues with Cloudbot handling replies

![AgentMail sponsorship demo](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/agentmail-sponsorship-demo.jpg)

The critical safety feature: **Cloudbot always asks for approval before sending any email.** Nothing goes out without your explicit sign-off. You can approve or adjust via voice memo, making it practical to handle multiple sponsorship negotiations simultaneously while staying in control.

## Use Case 6: Marketing Automation

![YouTube analytics showing Shorts performance](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/youtube-analytics-results.jpg)

When a new YouTube video is posted, Cloudbot automatically:

1. Detects the new upload (via Trigger Dev automation)
2. Sends the video to **Opus Clip** for AI-powered clipping
3. Publishes the resulting Shorts to YouTube, Instagram, and X using **Blotato**

The entire pipeline runs without manual intervention. Cloudbot built the automation itself — it wrote the Trigger Dev code, configured the Opus Clip integration, and set up the Blotato scheduling. The Shorts generated this way are getting meaningful views and subscribers.

This represents the concept of **agentic workflows**: Claude writing and running its own scripts on the always-on Mac mini. Because the Mac mini is a persistent server, automations don't stop when you close your laptop. Cloudbot maintains and monitors these workflows continuously.

## Use Case 7: QA Testing and Autonomous Code Fixes

This use case chains two capabilities together. First, Cloudbot acts as a QA tester:

- You tell it: *"Go to my website, check the footer links, and see if they're all directing properly."*
- Cloudbot opens the browser, systematically clicks through links, and reports issues via Telegram
- You can schedule this as a recurring cron job for continuous quality assurance

Then, because Cloudbot has been added as a GitHub collaborator with push access, it can fix the issues it finds:

- *"Go make the changes — fix those footer links. If someone hits Contact Us, direct them to our booking link."*
- Cloudbot writes the code changes and pushes them to the repository

The loop from detection to fix happens without you touching code or even opening a laptop.

## Use Case 8: Remote Access from Anywhere

![TG Watch app for Apple Watch](/blog/practical-cloudbot-use-cases/telegram-watch-app.jpg)

The final piece is access. Two tools make this work:

**TG Watch** — A Telegram client for Apple Watch ($-once purchase). Install it and you can send voice messages to Cloudbot directly from your wrist.

**Jump Desktop** — A remote desktop app ($15 one-time) that lets you see and control your Mac mini's screen from your iPhone or iPad. No subscription required. This is the tool for when you need to visually monitor what Cloudbot is doing or intervene when it gets stuck.

Together, these mean you have a powerful AI-powered computer that's always running automations, and you can monitor and control it from literally anywhere — your phone while commuting, your iPad on the couch, or your watch while walking.

## Keeping It Running 24/7

To ensure your Mac mini never sleeps:

1. Open **System Settings → Energy** and enable:
   - Prevent automatic sleeping when display is off
   - Wake for network access
   - Start up automatically after power failure
2. Ask Cloudbot to run `caffeinate` in the background as an extra safeguard

## Key Takeaways

- **Cloudbot is not "Claude on your phone"** — it's an autonomous agent with its own identity running on a persistent computer
- **Start cheap** — a used Mac mini or $25/month virtual Mac is enough
- **Proactive cron jobs** are the highest-impact first setup — daily check-ins change your productivity habits
- **Teach skills incrementally** — give Cloudbot API keys and let it build integrations itself, then save to soul.md
- **Always require approval** for external actions like sending emails
- **The Mac mini as a server** solves the persistence problem — automations run even when your laptop is off
- **Layer use cases** — browser automation + GitHub access + cron jobs compound into full QA-to-fix pipelines
